apps.name: Actual Budget
apps.short_description: Private, local-first envelope budgeting that gives every dollar a job and syncs across your devices.
apps.long_description:
## Overview
Actual Budget is a fast, local-first personal finance app built around
zero-based (envelope) budgeting: every dollar gets a job, so you always
know what your money is for. Budgets, accounts, and transactions live
entirely on your home server, and it stays snappy even with years of
history.

## Features
- Zero-based budgeting with multiple accounts, categories, and goals
- Scheduled and split transactions, plus custom rules to automate entry
- Reports to track spending and net worth over time
- Encrypted sync that keeps phones and laptops current with your server
- Optional automatic bank import so transactions show up on their own

## Setting up
On first visit, the server asks you to create a server password, which
then protects the whole instance:
- Password: set by you on first visit

## Good to know
Core budgeting is fully offline. Automatic bank import (via GoCardless or
SimpleFIN) is an advanced opt-in that needs internet access and your own
API keys from those providers.
apps.manifest:
id: actual-budget
manifest_version: 1
name: Actual Budget
version: "26.6.0"
description:
  short: "Private, local-first envelope budgeting that gives every dollar a job and syncs across your devices."
  long: |
    ## Overview
    Actual Budget is a fast, local-first personal finance app built around
    zero-based (envelope) budgeting: every dollar gets a job, so you always
    know what your money is for. Budgets, accounts, and transactions live
    entirely on your home server, and it stays snappy even with years of
    history.

    ## Features
    - Zero-based budgeting with multiple accounts, categories, and goals
    - Scheduled and split transactions, plus custom rules to automate entry
    - Reports to track spending and net worth over time
    - Encrypted sync that keeps phones and laptops current with your server
    - Optional automatic bank import so transactions show up on their own

    ## Setting up
    On first visit, the server asks you to create a server password, which
    then protects the whole instance:
    - Password: set by you on first visit

    ## Good to know
    Core budgeting is fully offline. Automatic bank import (via GoCardless or
    SimpleFIN) is an advanced opt-in that needs internet access and your own

icon: ./icon.png
categories: [personal, productivity]
author:
  name: Actual
  url: https://actualbudget.org
license: MIT
links:
  homepage: https://actualbudget.org
  source: https://github.com/actualbudget/actual
  support: https://actualbudget.org/docs

compose_file: compose.yml
main_service: actual-server
main_port: 5006
preferred_slugs: [actual, budget]
health_probe: /health

# Folderless app: the actual-server image has no USER directive and no
# privilege-dropping entrypoint, so it runs as root upstream. service_user
# gives it a dedicated malmo non-root identity (band [2100,2999]) with data/
# chowned to it — financial data shouldn't run as the brain's euid.
service_user: true

resources:
  recommended: { memory: 256M, cpu: 0.5 }

# Actual keeps everything it owns — the SQLite budget databases and uploaded
# files — under /data, with no separable regenerable cache, so the whole data
# bind is backed up. Budgets are stored in its own database rather than as files
# in a use-case folder (there is no finance folder in the taxonomy) and it has no
# external-library option, so it manages its own content (forfeits the
# files-first-class badge) instead of taking a folder grant.
storage:
  data_volumes: [./data]
  estimated_size: 1M
  app_managed_user_content: true

# Core budgeting is fully offline, so no internet/lan grant. Bank sync (GoCardless
# / SimpleFIN auto-import) is the only internet-dependent feature — an advanced
# opt-in needing egress + user-supplied API keys — and is left off by default.
permissions:
  internet: false
  lan: false

# Filled by `go run ./cmd/malmo manifest resolve catalog/actual-budget/manifest.yml`.
images:
  actualbudget/actual-server:26.6.0:
    digest: sha256:74385f8067f401e61f0be9e343c471705c42dfaa195295c40c5b2f15f4dcc9d4
    download_bytes: 112909196
    disk_bytes: 386638848
apps.compose:
# Actual Budget keeps all of its state — the SQLite budget databases and uploaded
# files — under /data. Upstream's compose published 5006 and bound ./actual-data
# there; malmo drops the host port (the brain routes to main_port) and binds the
# app state under ./data. The image creates a non-root `actual` user and chowns
# /data but never issues USER, so it runs as root upstream; under malmo it runs as
# the elected non-root UID with cap_drop: ALL — a plain Node app needing only write
# access to /data, which the brain pre-creates and chowns to that UID. Upstream's
# compose healthcheck shells `node scripts/health-check.js`, which fetches the
# app's own /health endpoint; malmo probes that same endpoint via the manifest
# health_probe instead, so no compose healthcheck is needed.
services:
  actual-server:
    image: actualbudget/actual-server:26.6.0
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data

apps.name: Baserow
apps.short_description: Build databases that feel like spreadsheets, a self-hosted Airtable alternative.
apps.long_description:
## Overview
Baserow turns your data into collaborative tables you edit like a
spreadsheet: add fields with real types, link tables into relationships, and
view the same records as a grid, gallery, kanban board, calendar, or form.
Everything lives in a database on your own box, and every table you build
gets a documented REST API for free. malmo provisions and manages the
database and cache Baserow needs, so there is nothing to wire up.

## Features
- Grid, gallery, kanban, calendar, and form views over the same records
- Real field types (dates, files, single and multiple select, ratings) plus
  formula and lookup fields that calculate across linked tables
- Link tables into relationships to build trackers, CRMs, inventories, and
  content calendars your whole team can edit at once
- Live collaboration: edits, comments, and presence show up as they happen
- An automatically generated REST API, with docs, over everything you build
- Automations and webhooks that fire when rows change
- Import from CSV, XML, JSON, Paste, or an existing Airtable base

## Setting up
The first account you register after install becomes the administrator.

## Good to know
Workspace invitations, password resets, and notification emails are sent by
email. Until an administrator adds an outgoing email account in malmo and
binds it to this app, those features quietly do nothing while everything
else works: you can still create accounts by registering them directly, and
everyone signs in with an email and password.

Baserow's optional AI assistant needs a Postgres vector extension that
malmo's managed database does not carry, so assistant search over your data
is unavailable. This affects only that assistant. Tables, views, formulas,
automations, and the API are all unaffected.

Baserow runs as several pieces (a web frontend, an API, three background
workers, and a router), so it is happier on a box with a few gigabytes of
memory to spare and takes a little longer to install than most apps.

manifest_version: 1
name: Baserow
version: "2.3.2"

    Everything lives in a database on your own box, and every table you build
    gets a documented REST API for free. malmo provisions and manages the
    database and cache Baserow needs, so there is nothing to wire up.

    ## Features

    - Real field types (dates, files, single and multiple select, ratings) plus

    - Link tables into relationships to build trackers, CRMs, inventories, and

    - An automatically generated REST API, with docs, over everything you build
    - Automations and webhooks that fire when rows change

    ## Setting up

icon: ./icon.png
categories: [developer-tools, productivity]
author:
  name: Baserow B.V.
  url: https://baserow.io
# Baserow Open Source Edition is MIT Expat. The repo is multi-licensed: the
# premium/ and enterprise/ directories carry their own source-available
# licenses, but those features are gated behind a paid license key and are not
# enabled here, so what we ship and run is the MIT OSE. No hosted-tier bar.
license: MIT
links:
  homepage: https://baserow.io
  source: https://github.com/baserow/baserow
  support: https://baserow.io/docs
changelog_url: https://gitlab.com/baserow/baserow/-/releases

compose_file: compose.yml
main_service: caddy
main_port: 8080
preferred_slugs: [baserow, tables, database]

# Caddy answers on :8080 the moment it is up, and the Nuxt frontend 302s at / as soon as it
# boots, so neither is an honest readiness signal: both are live minutes before the app is
# usable. /api/_health/ is the backend's own health endpoint and only answers once Django has
# applied the full migration set against the managed Postgres, which is the long pole on a
# cold first boot (measured ~2.5 min, and it is the only thing standing between install and
# a working app).
health_probe:
  path: /api/_health/
  start_period: 300s

# Baserow's images bake USER 9999:9999, but they do no root-first setup, no self-chown, and no
# privilege drop, so they honor whatever identity malmo pins instead of insisting on their own.
# That makes a dedicated non-root identity strictly available here, so take it rather than
# running the stack as the brain's uid. malmo pins ONE identity across all of an app's
# containers, so the whole stack has to tolerate it, and it does: verified booting, migrating,
# serving, and writing uploads into the shared media bind as an arbitrary uid under
# cap_drop: ALL + no-new-privileges, with zero permission errors across all six containers.
service_user: true

# Eight containers: gunicorn (3 workers), three resident celery processes, the Nuxt SSR
# frontend, and Caddy. The frontend and the API are the memory-hungry pair.
resources:
  recommended: { memory: 4G, cpu: 2.0 }

# Every table, row, view, formula, and automation lives in the managed Postgres database and
# is backed up through the managed-service path. What is on disk here: ./data/media is the
# user-file store (every attachment and image uploaded into a row, plus generated exports and
# thumbnails), shared by the backend, the workers that write exports, and Caddy which serves
# it back. The two caddy dirs are its own state and are scratch. Measured ~28KB at first
# healthy with one uploaded file; media grows entirely with what users attach. Baserow owns
# its file store internally with no external-library model, so this is app-managed content,
# not a use-case folder grant.
storage:
  data_volumes:
    - ./data/media
    - ./data/caddy-data
    - ./data/caddy-config
  estimated_size: 50MB
  app_managed_user_content: true

# Postgres holds everything; Valkey (declared as the redis alias) is the Celery broker AND
# the result/cache backend, plus redbeat's scheduler lock. Baserow needs both to boot: with
# no reachable broker the workers idle and every export, webhook, and automation silently
# never runs. Postgres 15 is upstream's own pin for this release line.
services:
  database:
    type: postgres
    version: "15"
  cache:
    type: redis
    version: "7"

# SECRET_KEY signs Django sessions and the password-reset tokens; BASEROW_JWT_SIGNING_KEY
# signs the API tokens. Upstream ships NO default for either (its compose declares both as
# required, `${SECRET_KEY:?}`), so both must be supplied or the app will not start. Both are
# re-emitted verbatim on restart, so live sessions and issued API tokens survive.
secrets:
  - name: secret_key
  - name: jwt_signing_key

# Workspace invitations, password resets, and row-notification emails. Mapped onto Baserow's
# EMAIL_SMTP_* family; unbound, Baserow falls back to Django's console mail backend and runs
# normally. See compose.yml for why the encryption flags are normalized in an entrypoint
# wrapper rather than mapped directly.
mail:
  optional: true

# internet: Baserow reaches out to external SMTP for mail, to arbitrary URLs for webhooks and
# data-sync sources, and to Airtable when a user imports a base. lan: not needed, the brain
# routes inbound traffic, and reaching a service on the local network is an opt-in power-user
# case we do not grant by default.
permissions:
  internet: true
  lan: false

images:
  baserow/backend:2.3.2:
    digest: sha256:bfa2d701231795cfbd665d7355a46d6b207f171e1bcb49e6f04cd58ac23d284e
    download_bytes: 375269659
    disk_bytes: 945354752
  baserow/web-frontend:2.3.2:
    digest: sha256:d616a12e66d6e172d504748c18400f1744fbc75d84b1bad44e41220483cf2591
    download_bytes: 107356986
    disk_bytes: 346151424
  caddy:2.11.4:
    digest: sha256:5f5c8640aae01df9654968d946d8f1a56c497f1dd5c5cda4cf95ab7c14d58648
    download_bytes: 23907283
    disk_bytes: 63392256
apps.compose:
# Baserow adapted for malmo's Tier-3 sandbox, from the upstream docker-compose.yml (v2.3.2).
#
# The all-in-one image (baserow/baserow) is deliberately NOT used, even though it is the
# shape upstream's README recommends. Its /baserow.sh runs
#   chown -R "$DOCKER_USER": "$DATA_DIR"/{caddy,media,env,backups}
# plus a su-exec privilege drop, under `set -euo pipefail`. Both need caps that cap_drop: ALL
# strips, and the chown is not guarded with `|| true`, so boot aborts outright (verified:
# `chown: changing ownership of '/baserow/data/redis': Operation not permitted`). That is the
# nonroot-data-ownership trap that took poznote and calibre-web. The split multi-container
# shape below has neither problem.
#
# malmo changes:
#  - db (pgvector/pgvector:pg15) dropped -> managed Postgres 15. See the pgvector note below:
#    the extension is optional and Baserow degrades gracefully without it.
#  - redis (redis:6) dropped -> managed Valkey 8 via the `redis:7` alias
#    (${MALMO_SERVICE_CACHE_DSN}, redis:// scheme).
#  - caddy KEPT and is load-bearing, not redundant. Baserow needs TWO browser-facing origins:
#    the Nuxt frontend, plus the Django backend for /api, /ws, /mcp, /assistant and /media.
#    malmo routes ONE main_port, so something has to path-route them onto a single origin,
#    and this is it.
#  - caddy's Caddyfile is INLINED via a heredoc rather than bind-mounted. Upstream binds
#    $PWD/Caddyfile from the repo; a catalog app ships a compose and a manifest, not side
#    files, so the config is written at boot instead. It is upstream's Caddyfile reduced to
#    the routes a malmo install actually uses (no on-demand TLS: malmo's own Caddy terminates
#    TLS in front of this one, and no BASEROW_CADDY_ADDRESSES host matching, since the brain
#    routes by Host into a single site).
#  - caddy entrypoint overridden to work around setcap vs cap_drop: ALL. /usr/bin/caddy carries
#    file capabilities (cap_net_bind_service=ep); with an empty bounding set the kernel refuses
#    to execve it AT ALL, for root and non-root alike:
#      exec /usr/bin/caddy: operation not permitted
#    Copying the binary drops the xattrs (cp preserves no capabilities), and the capability was
#    never needed here because the listen address is :8080. Same fix as plane's proxy. See
#    docs/admissibility-gate.md (Gate B, file-capability binaries).
#  - upstream's `volume-permissions-fixer` service (a bash:4.4 one-shot running
#    `chown 9999:9999 -R /baserow/media`) is DROPPED. The brain already creates and chowns every
#    declared relative bind to the runtime identity before compose up, so it is redundant, and
#    under cap_drop: ALL the chown would fail anyway.
#  - the backend/web-frontend images bake USER 9999:9999 but do no root-first setup and no
#    self-chown, so they honor the arbitrary uid malmo pins via service_user. Verified: the full
#    stack boots, migrates, and serves at uid 10001 under cap_drop: ALL + no-new-privileges.
#  - host `ports:` mappings dropped throughout; named volumes -> ./data/ binds.
#  - SECRET_KEY and BASEROW_JWT_SIGNING_KEY come from the manifest's `secrets:`. Upstream's
#    compose makes both required (`${SECRET_KEY:?}`) with no default, so both must be supplied.
#  - SYNC_TEMPLATES_ON_STARTUP is set to "false". Upstream defaults it to true, which imports
#    Baserow's full example-template library on first boot and adds several minutes to a cold
#    start for content most users never open. Templates can still be synced later from the
#    admin area.

x-backend-env: &backend-env
  # Managed Postgres (provisioned + injected by malmo). Baserow takes discrete fields; the
  # injected password is base64url and the database name is a sanitized SQL identifier, so
  # neither needs escaping here.
  DATABASE_HOST: ${MALMO_SERVICE_DATABASE_HOST}
  DATABASE_PORT: ${MALMO_SERVICE_DATABASE_PORT}
  DATABASE_USER: ${MALMO_SERVICE_DATABASE_USER}
  DATABASE_PASSWORD: ${MALMO_SERVICE_DATABASE_PASSWORD}
  DATABASE_NAME: ${MALMO_SERVICE_DATABASE_NAME}
  # Managed Valkey, injected as a redis:// DSN. Baserow reads REDIS_URL in preference to the
  # discrete REDIS_* fields.
  REDIS_URL: ${MALMO_SERVICE_CACHE_DSN}

  # Signs Django sessions (SECRET_KEY) and issues API tokens (BASEROW_JWT_SIGNING_KEY).
  # Upstream ships no defaults for either; both are CSPRNG values from the manifest's secrets:.
  SECRET_KEY: ${MALMO_SECRET_SECRET_KEY}
  BASEROW_JWT_SIGNING_KEY: ${MALMO_SECRET_JWT_SIGNING_KEY}

  # Public URL. All three must agree and must be the URL the BROWSER uses, because Baserow
  # bakes them into the frontend's API client, its CORS/CSRF allowlists, and share links.
  # The brain injects the public https:// URL on hosted and the .local URL on appliance.
  BASEROW_PUBLIC_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}
  PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}
  PUBLIC_WEB_FRONTEND_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}
  # malmo's Caddy terminates TLS and forwards X-Forwarded-Proto; without this Django builds
  # http:// URLs behind an https:// origin and the frontend trips CSRF on every write.
  BASEROW_ENABLE_SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER: "true"

  PRIVATE_BACKEND_URL: http://backend:8000
  MEDIA_ROOT: /baserow/media
  MEDIA_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}/media/

  # See the header note: upstream defaults this true and it dominates cold-start time.
  SYNC_TEMPLATES_ON_STARTUP: "false"
  MIGRATE_ON_STARTUP: "true"

  # Outgoing mail (manifest `mail:` block). Baserow only routes mail through SMTP when
  # EMAIL_SMTP is truthy, so unbound (the vars expand empty) it silently sends nothing and the
  # app runs normally, logging mail to the console backend instead. Bound, the brain injects
  # the MALMO_MAIL_* fields.
  EMAIL_SMTP: "${MALMO_MAIL_HOST:+yes}"
  EMAIL_SMTP_HOST: "${MALMO_MAIL_HOST:-}"
  EMAIL_SMTP_PORT: "${MALMO_MAIL_PORT:-}"
  EMAIL_SMTP_USER: "${MALMO_MAIL_USER:-}"
  EMAIL_SMTP_PASSWORD: "${MALMO_MAIL_PASSWORD:-}"
  FROM_EMAIL: "${MALMO_MAIL_FROM:-}"
  # The encryption mode is passed through RAW and normalized by the entrypoint wrapper below,
  # NOT mapped straight onto EMAIL_SMTP_USE_TLS / EMAIL_SMTP_USE_SSL. This is load-bearing.
  # Baserow reads those two as `bool(os.getenv(...))`, and in Python bool("false") is True, so
  # forwarding malmo's booleans verbatim would make BOTH read true. Baserow then raises
  # ImproperlyConfigured ("mutually exclusive and both cannot be set at once") and the backend
  # crash-loops -- triggered not by installing the app but by an admin binding a mail provider
  # later. Only the literal string "true" may turn a flag on; see x-mail-normalizing-entrypoint.
  #
  # These carry a NON-MALMO name on purpose. MALMO_* is the brain's reserved namespace and its
  # values live in the deploy-time .env, not in the container environment. Re-injecting under
  # the same name would squat that namespace and blur which side of the boundary a reader is
  # looking at. The rename keeps the two unambiguous: single-$ on the right is the deploy-time
  # value malmo interpolates, and the name on the left is what the container shell expands at
  # runtime (double-$ in the entrypoint below).
  SMTP_ENCRYPTION_USE_TLS: "${MALMO_MAIL_USE_TLS:-}"
  SMTP_ENCRYPTION_USE_SSL: "${MALMO_MAIL_USE_SSL:-}"

# Translates malmo's mail booleans into the only form Baserow reads safely, then hands off to
# the image's own entrypoint untouched. `bash -c '<script>' -- "$@"` puts the service's own
# command back in "$@", so each backend service keeps its distinct command (gunicorn,
# celery-worker, ...) while sharing this wrapper. Exporting a flag ONLY on the literal "true"
# is the whole point: any other value must leave the variable unset, because Baserow treats
# every non-empty string as true. Verified against a bound STARTTLS provider and an implicit
# TLS one, and with mail unbound.
x-mail-normalizing-entrypoint: &mail-normalizing-entrypoint
  - /bin/bash
  - -c
  # Every $ below is DOUBLED. These tokens must survive compose interpolation and reach the
  # shell at runtime; written as `${VAR}` / `"$@"` compose would expand them at deploy time,
  # baking in whatever the brain's environment held (or blanking them) and silently breaking
  # the normalization this wrapper exists to do. That is the openclaw interpolation bug, and
  # check-compose.py renders this file through real `docker compose config` to catch it.
  - |
    if [ "$${SMTP_ENCRYPTION_USE_SSL:-}" = "true" ]; then export EMAIL_SMTP_USE_SSL=yes; fi
    if [ "$${SMTP_ENCRYPTION_USE_TLS:-}" = "true" ]; then export EMAIL_SMTP_USE_TLS=yes; fi
    exec /usr/bin/tini -- /bin/bash /baserow/backend/docker/docker-entrypoint.sh "$$@"
  - --

services:
  # Path-routes the frontend and the backend onto one origin, and serves user-uploaded files
  # out of the shared media bind. This is the app's main_service.
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2.11.4
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    command:
      - |
        cat > /tmp/Caddyfile <<'CADDYEOF'
        :8080 {
          @backend_routes path /api/* /ws/* /mcp/* /assistant/*
          handle @backend_routes {
            reverse_proxy http://backend:8000
          }

          handle_path /media/* {
            @downloads query dl=*
            header @downloads Content-Disposition "attachment; filename={query.dl}"
            header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
            header Content-Security-Policy "sandbox; default-src 'none'; script-src 'none'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'"
            root * /baserow/media
            file_server
          }

          reverse_proxy http://web-frontend:3000
        }
        CADDYEOF
        cp /usr/bin/caddy /tmp/caddy
        exec /tmp/caddy run --config /tmp/Caddyfile --adapter caddyfile
    environment:
      XDG_DATA_HOME: /data
      XDG_CONFIG_HOME: /config
    volumes:
      - ./data/media:/baserow/media
      - ./data/caddy-data:/data
      - ./data/caddy-config:/config
    depends_on:
      - backend
      - web-frontend

  backend:
    image: baserow/backend:2.3.2
    entrypoint: *mail-normalizing-entrypoint
    command: ["gunicorn"]
    environment: *backend-env
    volumes:
      - ./data/media:/baserow/media
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/baserow/backend/docker/docker-entrypoint.sh backend-healthcheck"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 180s

  web-frontend:
    image: baserow/web-frontend:2.3.2
    environment:
      BASEROW_PUBLIC_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}
      PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}
      PUBLIC_WEB_FRONTEND_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}
      PRIVATE_BACKEND_URL: http://backend:8000
      MEDIA_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}/media/
      # Baserow refuses to start the frontend if it cannot reach PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL from
      # inside the container. On malmo that URL resolves through the box's public routing,
      # which is not reachable from within the app's own compose network at boot, so the
      # check is disabled; the backend is reached over PRIVATE_BACKEND_URL regardless.
      BASEROW_DISABLE_PUBLIC_URL_CHECK: "true"
    depends_on:
      - backend

  # General background work: exports, imports, webhooks, automation runs, trash cleanup.
  celery:
    image: baserow/backend:2.3.2
    entrypoint: *mail-normalizing-entrypoint
    command: ["celery-worker"]
    environment: *backend-env
    volumes:
      - ./data/media:/baserow/media
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/baserow/backend/docker/docker-entrypoint.sh celery-worker-healthcheck"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 180s
    depends_on:
      - backend

  # Dedicated queue for file exports so a large export cannot starve interactive jobs.
  celery-export-worker:
    image: baserow/backend:2.3.2
    entrypoint: *mail-normalizing-entrypoint
    command: ["celery-exportworker"]
    environment: *backend-env
    volumes:
      - ./data/media:/baserow/media
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/baserow/backend/docker/docker-entrypoint.sh celery-exportworker-healthcheck"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 180s
    depends_on:
      - backend

  # Scheduler for periodic jobs (field updates, retention cleanups).
  celery-beat-worker:
    image: baserow/backend:2.3.2
    entrypoint: *mail-normalizing-entrypoint
    command: ["celery-beat"]
    environment: *backend-env
    # Upstream sets this: redbeat needs SIGQUIT to release its scheduler lock on shutdown,
    # otherwise the next start waits out the stale lock.
    stop_signal: SIGQUIT
    # Upstream's compose overrides the healthcheck on the two celery workers but NOT on beat,
    # so beat inherits the image's baked HEALTHCHECK -- which probes the Django HTTP server that
    # beat does not run, leaving the container permanently `unhealthy` (observed). The image
    # ships a `celery-beat-healthcheck` command for exactly this; wire it up so the brain sees
    # honest health for every container in the app.
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/baserow/backend/docker/docker-entrypoint.sh celery-beat-healthcheck"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 5
      # Beat deliberately sleeps BASEROW_CELERY_BEAT_STARTUP_DELAY (15s default) before it
      # starts, on top of the backend's migration wait.
      start_period: 240s
    volumes:
      - ./data/media:/baserow/media
    depends_on:
      - backend

## Overview
Blinko is a quick-capture notebook built around small Markdown cards: open
it, jot the thought, done. Notes carry attachments, todos, and tags, and
everything lives in your home server's database.

## Features
- Fast card-style capture with Markdown, attachments, and todos
- Tag and full-text search across everything you've written
- Natural-language search over your notes when you connect an AI provider
- Desktop and mobile companion apps that sync to your instance

The first account you register after install becomes the administrator.

## Good to know
Natural-language (AI) search is optional and needs internet access plus your
own AI provider API key. Everything else runs fully offline; nothing leaves
your server unless you opt in.

icon: ./icon.png
screenshots: [./screenshots/01.png]
categories: [productivity]
author:
  name: Blinko
  url: https://blinko.space
license: GPL-3.0
links:
  homepage: https://blinko.space
  source: https://github.com/blinkospace/blinko
  support: https://docs.blinko.space
changelog_url: https://github.com/blinkospace/blinko/releases

compose_file: compose.yml
main_service: blinko
main_port: 1111
preferred_slugs: [blinko, notes]

# Unauthenticated "/" serves the app shell (200). First boot applies ~30
# Prisma migrations plus a seed against the managed Postgres before the
# server listens, so allow a margin on slow disks.
health_probe:
  path: /
  start_period: 120s

resources:
  recommended: { memory: 512M, cpu: 0.5 }

# Notes, accounts, and settings live in the managed Postgres; ./data is
# /app/.blinko — uploaded attachments (files/), installed plugins (plugins/),
# the app's own scheduled pg dumps (pgdump/), and the AI embeddings index
# (vector/). vector/ is rebuildable on demand and pgdump/ holds copies of
# data already protected by the managed-service backup path, so both are
# cache. Measured baseline at first healthy on a clean install is ~0 (four
# empty directories). Notes are database rows, not files in a use-case
# folder, and there is no external-library option, so the app manages its
# own content (forfeits the files-first-class badge).
storage:
  data_volumes: [./data]
  cache_volumes: [./data/vector, ./data/pgdump]
  estimated_size: 1M
  app_managed_user_content: true

services:
  database:
    type: postgres
    version: "15"

# Blinko signs auth tokens with NEXTAUTH_SECRET (the name survives from its
# earlier Next.js stack). The brain generates it once at install and injects
# MALMO_SECRET_AUTH; the compose maps it across, stable across restarts so
# sessions survive.
secrets:
  - name: auth

# internet: only for features the user opts into later — an external AI
# provider for the RAG search, the plugin marketplace, webhooks. Core note
# capture needs no outbound access. lan: not needed — the brain routes
# inbound traffic.
permissions:
  internet: true
  lan: false

# Filled by `go run ./cmd/malmo manifest resolve catalog/blinko/manifest.yml`.
images:
  blinkospace/blinko:1.8.7:
    digest: sha256:f7c1167f8c86db586599d849539a732929d89adb10977046e7b427813b2a84b4
    download_bytes: 435911817
    disk_bytes: 1250560000
apps.compose:
# Blinko adapted for malmo's Tier-3 sandbox (cap_drop: ALL, no-new-privileges,
# brain-pinned user:). Upstream's compose runs blinko + its own postgres:14 and
# publishes 1111; malmo drops the host port (the brain routes to main_port),
# drops the bundled database and declares managed Postgres in the manifest
# instead, and binds the app's state dir (/app/.blinko) under ./data.
#
# Verified live under the sandbox at a pinned non-root identity (uid 2100,
# cap_drop ALL): Prisma migrations + seed run against the managed-style DSN,
# the seed creates .blinko/{files,plugins,pgdump,vector} owned by the pinned
# UID, and the server answers 200 on :1111. No default account is seeded in
# production — the first registered user becomes the superadmin. Re-verify on
# version bumps.
services:
  blinko:
    image: blinkospace/blinko:1.8.7
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      # Auth-token signing secret (the NEXTAUTH_ name survives from Blinko's
      # earlier Next.js stack). Generated per-instance by the brain (manifest
      # `secrets: [{name: auth}]`) and injected as MALMO_SECRET_AUTH; stable
      # across restarts so sessions survive.
      NEXTAUTH_SECRET: ${MALMO_SECRET_AUTH}
      DATABASE_URL: ${MALMO_SERVICE_DATABASE_DSN}
    volumes:
      - ./data:/app/.blinko

apps.name: Chatto
apps.short_description: Self-hosted team and community chat with rooms, threads, and reactions.
apps.long_description:
## Overview
Chatto gives a team, a club, or a group of friends its own chat server, organized into channels and private rooms. It covers the essentials of a modern chat app while keeping every message on your own hardware instead of a vendor's servers.

## Features
- Channels and private rooms with threaded replies and reactions
- Mentions, file and image attachments, and full-text-searchable history
- Accounts created with an email address and a password
- A single lightweight Go process backed by NATS JetStream

## Setting up
Chatto sends a one-time verification code by email to create any account, so before anyone can sign up, an admin must bind an outgoing email provider under Settings -> Outgoing email. Once that's done, sign up with one of the owner email addresses configured at install time to become the server's administrator:
- Owner email: the address (or addresses) entered as "Owner email addresses" during install

## Good to know
Voice and video calls, and screensharing, are switched off: they need a media server holding open ports directly on the host, which this platform doesn't grant to apps. The call buttons simply aren't shown; text chat, threads, and attachments are unaffected.
apps.manifest:
id: chatto
manifest_version: 1
name: Chatto
version: "0.4.3"
description:
  short: "Self-hosted team and community chat with rooms, threads, and reactions."
  long: |
    ## Overview
    Chatto gives a team, a club, or a group of friends its own chat server, organized into channels and private rooms. It covers the essentials of a modern chat app while keeping every message on your own hardware instead of a vendor's servers.

    ## Features
    - Channels and private rooms with threaded replies and reactions
    - Mentions, file and image attachments, and full-text-searchable history
    - Accounts created with an email address and a password
    - A single lightweight Go process backed by NATS JetStream

    ## Setting up
    Chatto sends a one-time verification code by email to create any account, so before anyone can sign up, an admin must bind an outgoing email provider under Settings -> Outgoing email. Once that's done, sign up with one of the owner email addresses configured at install time to become the server's administrator:
    - Owner email: the address (or addresses) entered as "Owner email addresses" during install

    ## Good to know
    Voice and video calls, and screensharing, are switched off: they need a media server holding open ports directly on the host, which this platform doesn't grant to apps. The call buttons simply aren't shown; text chat, threads, and attachments are unaffected.
icon: ./icon.png
categories: [productivity]
author:
  name: Chatto Corp
  url: https://chatto.run
license: AGPL-3.0-or-later
links:
  homepage: https://chatto.run
  source: https://github.com/chattocorp/chatto
  support: https://docs.chatto.run
changelog_url: https://github.com/chattocorp/chatto/releases

compose_file: compose.yml
main_service: chatto
main_port: 4000
preferred_slugs: [chatto, chat]

# /readyz is Chatto's own readiness probe: 200 once NATS is connected and every
# JetStream projection has caught up, 503 before that. Boot to first-ready was
# ~2s on a warm image; the grace covers the first-run NATS store creation and
# the RBAC/room seeding that runs with it.
health_probe:
  path: /readyz
  start_period: 60s

# The stock image starts as root and su-execs down to a baked `chatto` user —
# which cap_drop: ALL forbids (see compose.yml). Both services adopt whatever
# `user:` they are given, so a malmo-allocated identity owning ./data/nats is
# all that is needed; verified booting as an arbitrary non-root uid under
# cap_drop: ALL.
service_user: true

# One Go binary plus a NATS server. ffmpeg ships in the image and transcodes
# uploaded media on demand, which is the CPU spike worth budgeting for.
resources:
  recommended: { memory: 1G, cpu: 1.0 }

# Chatto is stateless: every stream, KV bucket, and object store — accounts,
# rooms, messages, and the attachments themselves — lives in the NATS JetStream
# store, so ./data/nats is the whole backup surface (docs: "Back up nats_data").
# Measured 140KB at first ready. Chat history is Chatto's own store rather than
# files in a use-case folder, and it offers no external-library option, so it
# manages its own content (forfeits the files-first-class badge).
storage:
  data_volumes: [./data/nats]
  estimated_size: 10MB
  app_managed_user_content: true

# Four token-signing secrets plus the NATS auth token. The four CHATTO_* ones
# must reach the app hex-encoded and 32 bytes wide, which base64url injection
# can't express — compose derives them as sha256(seed). See compose.yml.
secrets:
  - name: core_key
  - name: assets_signing
  - name: cookie_signing
  - name: cookie_encryption
  - name: nats_token

# Chatto grants owner (full admin) rights to whoever registers with one of these
# addresses, once the address is verified. There is no other way in: the first
# account is created through the normal sign-up form, and without a match nobody
# on the server can reach /admin.
config:
  - app_env: CHATTO_OWNERS_EMAILS
    title: Owner email addresses
    description: "Comma-separated emails that get owner rights on this server. Sign up with one of these to become the administrator."
    required: true

# Registration, email verification, and password reset all deliver a one-time
# code by email. Chatto has no other sign-up path, so until an admin binds an
# outgoing-mail provider the sign-up form answers 500 and no account — not even
# the first owner's — can be created. Declared optional because manifest v1 has
# no required-mail semantics and every app must install unbound.
mail:
  optional: true

# Outbound: SMTP delivery, link-preview fetches from the message composer, and
# OAuth/OIDC token exchange if an operator wires up an external login provider.
# Nothing inbound from the LAN.
permissions:
  internet: true
  lan: false

# Filled by `go run ./cmd/malmo manifest resolve apps/chatto/manifest.yml`.
images:
  ghcr.io/chattocorp/chatto:0.4.3:
    digest: sha256:6bf5ec391de5b2c47c78875accd691aa25b5c6d6a4f72c663514e49cd37ed5d3
    download_bytes: 90988846
    disk_bytes: 247170560
  nats:2.12-alpine:
    digest: sha256:2ca98656a279b2d88cfdf2b8c3f0d5d7f3941ae9dc2ab12ebaa92d83e0f4ccdb
    download_bytes: 10856577
    disk_bytes: 27575808
apps.compose:
# Chatto adapted for malmo's Tier-3 sandbox, from examples/dockercompose/compose.yml.
# malmo changes:
#  - `livekit` service dropped. It needs host UDP port bindings (50000-50200/udp
#    media, 3478/udp TURN/STUN) that malmo's admission policy rejects
#    unconditionally, and the app's own docs say avoiding them needs "a dedicated
#    IP address or host" — which a single shared Caddy ingress can't give per app.
#    Chatto documents `livekit.enabled = false` as a supported mode (call controls
#    hide, call APIs return null, chat is untouched), so we ship that way:
#    CHATTO_LIVEKIT_ENABLED=false. Voice/video calls + screensharing are off.
#  - `caddy` service dropped: it only terminated TLS and proxied to chatto:4000 and
#    livekit:7880. malmo's own ingress does that, so it is redundant here.
#  - nats: named volume `nats_data` -> relative bind ./data/nats; the host port
#    mappings and `latest` tag are gone. ALL chat state (streams, KV, object store
#    for attachments) lives in this one bind — chatto itself is stateless, which is
#    why it declares no data bind of its own.
#  - chatto: the stock entrypoint is bypassed. It starts as root, remaps its baked
#    `chatto` user with usermod/groupmod to PUID/PGID, then su-execs down — the
#    `nonroot-data-ownership` shape (as `jotty`, `postiz`). su-exec needs
#    CAP_SETGID/CAP_SETUID, which malmo's cap_drop: ALL strips. Instead the
#    manifest asks for `service_user: true` and we exec /chatto directly under the
#    identity malmo allocates. The only thing the entrypoint does besides the
#    privilege dance is write a nats-CLI context for `docker exec … nats`, which is
#    not a path a malmo user has.
#  - Secrets. Chatto requires three secrets that must be HEX and decode to exactly
#    32 bytes (config.go validateHexSecret: core.secret_key,
#    core.assets.signing_secret, webserver.cookie_signing_secret — the app refuses
#    to boot otherwise), plus an optional hex cookie-encryption key. malmo's
#    `secrets:` mechanism injects base64url, which hex.DecodeString rejects. So the
#    four MALMO_SECRET_* values arrive as CHATTO_SEED_* and the wrapper below
#    derives each app-facing secret as sha256(seed) -> 64 hex chars. The seeds are
#    32-byte CSPRNG values re-emitted stably across restarts, so the derived
#    secrets are stable too — rotating them would invalidate live sessions, bearer
#    tokens, and signed asset URLs. See the PR's Platform gaps (`secret-format`).
#    `$$` is a literal `$` for the shell: a bare `${…}` in a command block-scalar
#    is interpolated at deploy time by compose, not by sh.
#  - CHATTO_WEBSERVER_URL -> ${MALMO_APP_URL}: chatto builds absolute URLs (OAuth
#    callbacks, email links, asset URLs) from it and rejects a non-http(s) value.
#  - NATS auth token: upstream's operator-chosen NATS_TOKEN, from the same CSPRNG
#    mechanism. The nats server is only reachable on the instance's private compose
#    network, but the token is kept as defense in depth, matching upstream. It
#    does ride argv (visible to `docker inspect`), because nats-server takes the
#    token only as a flag or from a config file — a shell wrapper would exec the
#    same flag. Accepted: reading a container's argv needs box-root, which already
#    reads the instance .env the token is injected from. Unlike the four CHATTO_*
#    secrets below, which never leave the environment.
#  - Outgoing mail (manifest `mail:`). CHATTO_SMTP_ENABLED is gated on a provider
#    being bound, the established `${MALMO_MAIL_HOST:+true}` pattern (gitea, kimai,
#    paperless-ngx). Unbound, every CHATTO_SMTP_* below expands to the empty
#    string; chatto's env parser (caarlos0/env v11) skips empty values outright
#    (`if value != ""`), so the zero config stands and SMTP stays off. CHATTO_SMTP_TLS
#    is left to chatto's own default (mandatory STARTTLS, or implicit TLS on 465):
#    malmo's MALMO_MAIL_USE_TLS / MALMO_MAIL_USE_SSL are two booleans and chatto
#    wants one enum, so port 465 is the only reliable signal, and that is exactly
#    what TLSPolicyOrDefault() keys on.
#  - CHATTO_OWNERS_EMAILS is not set here: it is a manifest `config:` field, so the
#    brain stamps the user's answer straight into this service's override env.
services:
  nats:
    image: nats:2.12-alpine
    command: ["--jetstream", "--store_dir=/data", "--auth=${MALMO_SECRET_NATS_TOKEN}"]
    volumes:
      - ./data/nats:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "nats-server", "--help"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3

  chatto:
    image: ghcr.io/chattocorp/chatto:0.4.3
    depends_on:
      nats:
        condition: service_healthy
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    command:
      - |
        set -eu
        hex() { printf '%s' "$$1" | sha256sum | cut -c1-64; }
        export CHATTO_CORE_SECRET_KEY="$$(hex "$$CHATTO_SEED_CORE_KEY")"
        export CHATTO_CORE_ASSETS_SIGNING_SECRET="$$(hex "$$CHATTO_SEED_ASSETS_SIGNING")"
        export CHATTO_WEBSERVER_COOKIE_SIGNING_SECRET="$$(hex "$$CHATTO_SEED_COOKIE_SIGNING")"
        export CHATTO_WEBSERVER_COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_SECRET="$$(hex "$$CHATTO_SEED_COOKIE_ENCRYPTION")"
        exec /chatto start
    environment:
      CHATTO_SEED_CORE_KEY: ${MALMO_SECRET_CORE_KEY}
      CHATTO_SEED_ASSETS_SIGNING: ${MALMO_SECRET_ASSETS_SIGNING}
      CHATTO_SEED_COOKIE_SIGNING: ${MALMO_SECRET_COOKIE_SIGNING}
      CHATTO_SEED_COOKIE_ENCRYPTION: ${MALMO_SECRET_COOKIE_ENCRYPTION}

      CHATTO_WEBSERVER_URL: ${MALMO_APP_URL}
      CHATTO_WEBSERVER_PORT: "4000"

      CHATTO_NATS_EMBEDDED_ENABLED: "false"
      CHATTO_NATS_CLIENT_URL: nats://nats:4222
      CHATTO_NATS_CLIENT_AUTH_METHOD: token
      CHATTO_NATS_CLIENT_TOKEN: ${MALMO_SECRET_NATS_TOKEN}

      CHATTO_LIVEKIT_ENABLED: "false"
      CHATTO_LOG_LEVEL: info
      CHATTO_LOG_FORMAT: json

      CHATTO_SMTP_ENABLED: "${MALMO_MAIL_HOST:+true}"
      CHATTO_SMTP_HOST: "${MALMO_MAIL_HOST:-}"
      CHATTO_SMTP_PORT: "${MALMO_MAIL_PORT:-}"
      CHATTO_SMTP_USERNAME: "${MALMO_MAIL_USER:-}"
      CHATTO_SMTP_PASSWORD: "${MALMO_MAIL_PASSWORD:-}"
      CHATTO_SMTP_FROM: "${MALMO_MAIL_FROM:-}"

apps.name: Cube
apps.short_description: Open-source semantic layer that turns your data warehouse into one consistent metrics API for BI, embedded analytics, and AI.
apps.long_description:
## Overview
Cube is a headless semantic layer that sits in front of a data warehouse you
already run, such as Postgres, MySQL, ClickHouse, BigQuery, or Snowflake.
Define your metrics, dimensions, and access rules once, in version-controlled
data models, then serve them through a single consistent REST, GraphQL, and
SQL API. Every dashboard, embedded chart, and AI agent that queries Cube gets
the same definition of "revenue" or "active users."

## Features
- One consistent metrics API for dashboards, embedded analytics, and AI agents
- REST, GraphQL, and SQL access to the same data models
- Bundled Cube Store handles caching and pre-aggregations, so heavy queries
  stay fast without hammering your warehouse
- Version-controlled, config-as-code data models

## Setting up
Enter your warehouse connection (type, host, port, database, user, password)
in this app's configuration form at install or later under settings. Data
models are config-as-code, so write them by editing files under the app's
data directory rather than through an in-app editor.

Cube's API is authenticated with a signing secret malmo generates for you.
Find it in the app's settings to mint signed tokens for clients that query
the API.

## Good to know
Cube runs in production mode on malmo, the secure way to self-host it: the
Developer Playground (Cube's in-browser data model builder) only works in
development mode, which turns off API authentication, so malmo doesn't
enable it. Cube here is an API service, not a browsable dashboard.

Warehouses with their own credential model, such as BigQuery service-account
JSON or Snowflake account/warehouse variables, aren't covered by the
configuration form yet. Host-based warehouses (Postgres, MySQL, ClickHouse,
Redshift, Materialize) work fully.

icon: ./icon.svg
categories: [developer-tools]
author:
  name: Cube Dev
  url: https://cube.dev
license: Apache-2.0
links:
  homepage: https://cube.dev
  source: https://github.com/cube-js/cube
  support: https://cube.dev/docs
changelog_url: https://github.com/cube-js/cube/releases

compose_file: compose.yml
main_service: cube
main_port: 4000
preferred_slugs: [cube, semantic-layer, analytics]

# /livez is Cube's Kubernetes-style liveness endpoint on the API port; it flips
# healthy once the API server is up. Liveness, not /readyz, so the install gate
# tracks "Cube booted and serves HTTP" rather than the reachability of the
# external warehouse the user supplies (/readyz reports DOWN until a data source
# is connected). The cube image is large (~1.1 GB on disk) so the cold start is
# slower, and Cube Store builds its metastore on first boot — allow a generous
# start period.
health_probe:
  path: /livez
  start_period: 60s

# Cube's node API and the Rust Cube Store both sit idle-light but the JVM-free
# node stack plus Cube Store's in-memory pre-aggregation engine want headroom on
# the low-end hardware malmo targets; 1.5 GB keeps both comfortable before any
# large pre-aggregation build.
resources:
  recommended: { memory: 1536M, cpu: 1 }

# ./data/conf is Cube's config directory — the user-authored data models and
# cube config (config-as-code); it must be backed up. ./data/cubestore is Cube
# Store's pre-aggregation materializations and metadata, regenerable from the
# source warehouse, so it is cache. The user's actual analytics data never lives
# here — it stays in the external warehouse Cube queries. estimated_size measured
# at first-healthy on a clean boot with no data models authored yet.
storage:
  data_volumes: [./data/conf]
  cache_volumes: [./data/cubestore]
  estimated_size: 1M

# Cube requires an API signing secret in production mode (CUBEJS_API_SECRET); it
# signs and verifies the JWTs that authenticate every API call. The brain
# generates it once at install and injects it as MALMO_SECRET_API; the owner can
# read it to mint signed tokens for clients that query the API.
secrets:
  - name: api

# The data-source connection is the operator's own warehouse — malmo can neither
# generate these values nor ship them, so they're collected as config fields
# (APP_MANIFEST.md # D4) and injected verbatim under Cube's own env-var names (no
# MALMO_* indirection) into the cube service. These cover Cube's host-based
# drivers (Postgres, MySQL, ClickHouse, Redshift, Materialize, …); warehouses
# with their own credential model (BigQuery service-account JSON, Snowflake
# account/warehouse) use driver-specific variables not on this form yet — see the
# Platform gaps note on the PR. CUBEJS_DB_TYPE is required so the app never
# installs without a declared warehouse type; the connection params are optional
# because the required subset differs per driver, and Cube reads whichever are
# set. Targets main_service (cube) by default — no `service:` needed.
config:
  - app_env: CUBEJS_DB_TYPE
    title: "Data source type"
    description: "Which warehouse Cube connects to, e.g. postgres, mysql, clickhouse, redshift, materialize. See cube.dev/docs for the full driver list and any driver-specific variables."
    required: true
  - app_env: CUBEJS_DB_HOST
    title: "Database host"
    description: "Hostname or IP of your warehouse, reachable from your home server (a LAN address or a cloud endpoint)."
  - app_env: CUBEJS_DB_PORT
    title: "Database port"
    description: "Port your warehouse listens on. Leave blank to use the driver's default (e.g. 5432 for Postgres)."
  - app_env: CUBEJS_DB_NAME
    title: "Database name"
    description: "The database (or schema/dataset) Cube queries."
  - app_env: CUBEJS_DB_USER
    title: "Database user"
    description: "Username Cube authenticates to the warehouse with."
  - app_env: CUBEJS_DB_PASS
    title: "Database password"
    description: "Password for the database user. Leave blank if your warehouse uses passwordless/trust auth."
    secret: true
  - app_env: CUBEJS_DB_SSL
    title: "Use SSL/TLS"
    description: "Encrypt the connection to the warehouse. Enable for cloud warehouses that require TLS."
    type: bool
    default: "false"

# internet: warehouses are routinely cloud-hosted (BigQuery, Snowflake, a managed
# Postgres), which Cube must reach to answer queries. lan: a self-hosted
# warehouse is just as often another box on the home network. Cube connects
# outward to whichever the user configures; the brain still routes all inbound.
permissions:
  internet: true
  lan: true

images:
  cubejs/cube:v1.6.64:
    digest: sha256:42418fc85830763178abd45ca93e60fefec27effb92418f9d977699bc38483f5
    download_bytes: 332624667
    disk_bytes: 1083945984
  cubejs/cubestore:v1.6.64:
    digest: sha256:6494961cd5de30bba97608ad46ed5e164adf23eeb211f0ebcfcce7e9b56251ff
    download_bytes: 95248729
    disk_bytes: 265027072
apps.compose:
# Cube adapted for malmo's Tier-3 sandbox (cap_drop: ALL, no-new-privileges,
# brain-pinned non-root user:). Upstream's production compose is a five-service
# scale-out (a Cube API instance, a refresh worker, a Cube Store router, and two
# Cube Store workers) that publishes host port 4000. malmo drops the host port
# (the brain routes to main_port 4000) and collapses the cluster to the smallest
# stack that runs a real semantic layer: one Cube API container plus a single
# Cube Store node. The refresh worker is folded away — pre-aggregations refresh
# in-process for a single-instance home deployment — and the two Cube Store
# workers collapse into the one standalone node, which is how Cube Store runs
# when no CUBESTORE_WORKERS list is set.
#
# Production mode, never dev mode. CUBEJS_DEV_MODE is pinned false: dev mode
# disables Cube's API authentication entirely and exposes the Developer
# Playground, which on a routable app URL is an unauthenticated query gateway to
# the connected warehouse. The cost is that the Playground UI is dev-only — a
# production Cube is a headless REST/GraphQL/SQL API with no web dashboard.
#
# Env rewiring (the brain injects the values; the compose maps them to Cube's
# own names):
#   CUBEJS_API_SECRET  -> ${MALMO_SECRET_API}   (CSPRNG, generated once at
#                                                install; signs/verifies the API
#                                                JWTs Cube requires in production)
#   CUBEJS_CUBESTORE_HOST/PORT                   point the API at the bundled
#                                                single Cube Store node
#
# The data-source connection (CUBEJS_DB_TYPE + CUBEJS_DB_* credentials) is the
# operator's own warehouse, which malmo can neither generate nor ship. Those are
# declared as `config:` fields in the manifest (APP_MANIFEST.md # D4) and the
# brain stamps each one into this service's environment override under its own
# name (CUBEJS_DB_HOST, CUBEJS_DB_PASS, ...), so they are not listed here.
services:
  cube:
    image: cubejs/cube:v1.6.64
    depends_on:
      - cubestore
    environment:
      CUBEJS_DEV_MODE: "false"
      CUBEJS_API_SECRET: ${MALMO_SECRET_API}
      CUBEJS_CUBESTORE_HOST: cubestore
      CUBEJS_CUBESTORE_PORT: "3030"
    volumes:
      # Cube loads its data models and config from /cube/conf — the user-authored
      # semantic layer, kept across restarts. App state, not user content.
      - ./data/conf:/cube/conf
    # The image ships node but no curl/wget, so probe /livez (Cube's
    # Kubernetes-style liveness endpoint) with the bundled node runtime. Liveness
    # rather than /readyz so the install gate tracks "Cube booted and serves
    # HTTP", not the reachability of an external warehouse the user supplies.
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "node", "-e", "require('http').get('http://localhost:4000/livez',r=>process.exit(r.statusCode<500?0:1)).on('error',()=>process.exit(1))"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 18
      start_period: 60s

  cubestore:
    image: cubejs/cubestore:v1.6.64
    volumes:
      # Single standalone node (no CUBESTORE_WORKERS): Cube Store persists its
      # RocksDB metastore and pre-aggregation materializations under its default
      # data dir, /cube/.cubestore. That baked path is unwritable to the non-root
      # sandbox uid, so bind it — otherwise Cube Store panics on startup trying to
      # create the metastore directory. The contents are regenerable from the
      # source warehouse, so the bind is declared cache, not backed-up data.
      - ./data/cubestore:/cube/.cubestore

apps.name: DocuSeal
apps.short_description: Self-hosted PDF document signing and form filling.
apps.long_description:
## Overview
DocuSeal lets you create fillable PDF forms, collect legally binding
e-signatures, and manage the full signing workflow from a single
dashboard, without routing documents through a third-party cloud.
Documents and signatures live entirely on your own hardware.

## Features
- Visual drag-and-drop editor for building fillable PDF templates
- Automatic e-signature capture with signature verification
- Signature requests sent to multiple recipients by email
- Completed PDFs downloadable once every signer is done
- User management and role administration
- API and webhooks for integrating with other tools

## Setting up
The first account you register after install becomes the administrator.

Sending signature requests by email only works once an administrator adds
an outgoing email account under malmo's Settings → Outgoing email and
binds DocuSeal to it; DocuSeal's own built-in email settings page isn't
used.

## Good to know
Email-based signing is currently limited: signature-request links point to
this app's local network address, so a recipient can only open them from a
device on your home network. Links sent to people off your network won't
resolve until remote access is available. Use DocuSeal on your LAN, or
share completed documents another way.

apps.compose:
# DocuSeal (Rails) adapted for malmo's Tier-3 sandbox. The single ./data/app
# bind holds uploaded documents, generated PDFs, and signatures; the database is
# a managed Postgres declared in the manifest (the brain injects the DSN).
#
# Outgoing mail (manifest `mail:` block, #122). DocuSeal reads a full set of
# SMTP_* env vars at boot (config/environments/production.rb): once SMTP_ADDRESS
# is set ActionMailer switches to :smtp, and these env settings take precedence
# over DocuSeal's own in-app Email SMTP page (the DB-stored fallback). The brain
# injects the discrete MALMO_MAIL_* fields when an instance is bound to a
# provider, and the mapping below projects them onto DocuSeal's names:
# - SMTP_FROM is mandatory once SMTP is active — DocuSeal's mail interceptor
#   (lib/action_mailer_configs_interceptor.rb) does ENV.fetch('SMTP_FROM') with
#   no default and raises without it; it maps to MALMO_MAIL_FROM.
# - Encryption: DocuSeal takes two independent flags. SMTP_ENABLE_STARTTLS
#   defaults to ON (disabled only by the literal "false"), so it's driven
#   explicitly from MALMO_MAIL_USE_TLS (the brain's STARTTLS projection);
#   SMTP_ENABLE_SSL (implicit TLS / SMTPS) is driven from MALMO_MAIL_USE_SSL.
#   The two booleans are mutually exclusive, matching DocuSeal's expectation.
# Unbound, MALMO_MAIL_* are absent and the defaults below leave the SMTP_* vars
# empty. An empty SMTP_ADDRESS is still truthy to DocuSeal's boot check, so
# ActionMailer sits in :smtp mode with no real settings — but DocuSeal gates
# every send-email path (UI views and the invitation job) on can_send_emails?,
# which is false until a provider is bound, so no mail is offered or sent while
# unbound. The one consequence is that DocuSeal's own in-app Email SMTP page is
# shadowed (ignored) until a malmo provider is bound; outgoing mail is meant to
# be configured through Settings -> Outgoing email, not the app's page.
services:
  app:
    image: docuseal/docuseal:3.0.2
    volumes:
      - ./data/app:/data/docuseal
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: ${MALMO_SERVICE_DATABASE_DSN}
      SMTP_ADDRESS: "${MALMO_MAIL_HOST:-}"
      SMTP_PORT: "${MALMO_MAIL_PORT:-587}"
      SMTP_USERNAME: "${MALMO_MAIL_USER:-}"
      SMTP_PASSWORD: "${MALMO_MAIL_PASSWORD:-}"
      SMTP_FROM: "${MALMO_MAIL_FROM:-}"
      SMTP_ENABLE_STARTTLS: "${MALMO_MAIL_USE_TLS:-false}"
      SMTP_ENABLE_SSL: "${MALMO_MAIL_USE_SSL:-false}"

apps.name: Firecrawl
apps.short_description: Turn any website into clean, LLM-ready markdown or structured data with a self-hosted scraping and crawling API.
apps.long_description:
## Overview
Firecrawl is a web-scraping and crawling API that turns any URL, or a whole
site, into clean markdown or structured JSON, ready to feed an LLM, a RAG
pipeline, or an AI agent. It renders JavaScript with a real headless browser,
follows links to crawl entire sites, and hands back parsed content over a
simple HTTP API. This is an API service with no web dashboard to log into:
you drive it from your own code, an agent framework, or the official SDKs,
pointing them at this instance's URL.

## Features
- `/scrape` a single URL to markdown, HTML, or a structured extract
- `/crawl` a whole site, following links, with per-job status
- `/map` a site's URLs quickly without fetching every page
- Real headless-Chromium rendering for JavaScript-heavy pages
- Optional LLM-powered `/extract` (structured data from a schema or prompt)
  once you add an OpenAI-compatible API key
- Optional web `/search` once you point it at a SearXNG endpoint
- malmo provisions and manages the cache Firecrawl needs, so there is nothing
  to wire up for the core scraping API

## Good to know
- **LLM and search features are off until you configure them.** `/extract`
  and other LLM-backed extraction need an OpenAI-compatible API key, and
  `/search` needs a SearXNG endpoint. Set them on the app's page after
  install. Core scrape, crawl, and map work without either.
- **This is a heavy app.** It runs a Node API, a headless-Chromium browser
  service, a message broker, and a bundled Postgres alongside malmo's managed
  cache. That is several gigabytes to download and a few gigabytes of memory
  to run comfortably. Give it a box with room to spare, and large crawls want
  more.
- **Firecrawl has no login of its own, so keep it private.** malmo already
  keeps each app owner-only by default: the box login sits in front, so only
  you can reach this API. Leave it that way unless you specifically want an
  open, unauthenticated scraping endpoint, since anyone who can reach it can
  use it to fetch arbitrary URLs on your behalf.

icon: ./icon.png
categories: [developer-tools, ai]
author:
  name: Firecrawl
  url: https://firecrawl.dev
# AGPL-3.0. We ship the published upstream images unmodified, so the network-use
# source-offer obligation is satisfied by upstream; no hosted-tier bar.
license: AGPL-3.0
links:
  homepage: https://firecrawl.dev
  source: https://github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl
  support: https://docs.firecrawl.dev
changelog_url: https://github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl/releases

compose_file: compose.yml
main_service: api
main_port: 3002

# "scrape"/"crawl" are the verbs users reach for; "firecrawl" is the fallback.
preferred_slugs: [firecrawl, scrape, crawl]

# GET / is an unauthenticated liveness route the api serves as soon as Express is up
# ("SCRAPERS-JS: Hello, world!"). The api is the long pole on cold boot (Node + worker
# threads + the harness), measured ready ~30-40s; 120s leaves comfortable margin.
health_probe:
  path: /
  start_period: 120s

# FORCED, and the app's load-bearing field. Firecrawl needs two bundled infrastructure
# sidecars malmo does not provision as managed services: RabbitMQ (no managed AMQP type)
# and a CUSTOM postgres:17 + pg_cron + nuq.sql image the managed Postgres cannot replace.
# Both official images self-chown their data dir and gosu/privilege-drop ONLY when started
# as root; under cap_drop: ALL that root path dies (`chown: … Operation not permitted`).
# Run as an arbitrary non-root uid over a pre-chowned bind they skip both and boot clean.
# malmo pins ONE identity across all of an app's containers, so the whole stack must tolerate
# it, and it does. Verified booting the full stack (api + playwright + rabbitmq + nuq-postgres)
# as a non-root uid under cap_drop: ALL + no-new-privileges: nuq-postgres healthy with pg_cron
# running, rabbitmq healthy, chromium (--no-sandbox) serving rendered HTML, and an end-to-end
# /v1/scrape returning markdown, zero permission errors. The one non-root snag was the browser
# service's corepack cache (HOME=/), fixed with HOME=/tmp in compose.yml; see notes.md.
service_user: true

# Node API (with worker threads), a headless-Chromium browser service, a RabbitMQ broker, and
# a bundled Postgres, atop malmo's managed Valkey. Upstream caps the api at 8G and the browser
# at 4G for heavy crawling; a modest instance runs in less, but give it room.
resources:
  recommended: { memory: 8G, cpu: 4.0 }

# On disk: ./data/nuq-postgres is the bundled Postgres cluster that holds Firecrawl's job/queue
# state (the "nuq" queue schema + pg_cron housekeeping); ./data/rabbitmq is the broker's mnesia
# state. Both are operational stores, not user content; scraped results are returned over the
# API, not durably persisted here. Measured ~42MB at first-healthy after a few scrapes.
storage:
  data_volumes:
    - ./data/nuq-postgres
    - ./data/rabbitmq
  estimated_size: 50MB
  app_managed_user_content: false

# The queue/rate-limit/session store. Upstream ships Redis; malmo provisions managed Valkey
# (RESP-wire-compatible; verified Firecrawl's ioredis/BullMQ clients connect and drive the
# queue against it). REDIS_URL and REDIS_RATE_LIMIT_URL both map to MALMO_SERVICE_CACHE_DSN.
services:
  cache:
    type: valkey
    version: "8"

# postgres_password authenticates the api to the bundled nuq-postgres over the compose network;
# rabbitmq_password is the named broker user's password (the api's AMQP URL carries it). Neither
# leaves the compose network. Named credentials are required because RabbitMQ refuses its built-in
# guest user over a non-loopback connection.
secrets:
  - name: postgres_password
  - name: rabbitmq_password

# Optional operator integrations, injected onto the api when supplied. Unset -> the feature is
# simply off (core scrape/crawl/map unaffected), which is why neither is required.
config:
  - app_env: OPENAI_API_KEY
    title: OpenAI API key
    description: >
      Enables the LLM-backed /extract endpoint and other AI extraction features. An
      OpenAI key (or any OpenAI-compatible key). Leave blank to keep those features off.
    secret: true
    required: false
  - app_env: SEARXNG_ENDPOINT
    title: SearXNG endpoint URL
    description: >
      Enables the /search endpoint by pointing Firecrawl at a SearXNG instance you run
      (e.g. https://searxng.example.com). Leave blank to keep /search off.
    required: false

# internet: Firecrawl's entire job is fetching arbitrary external URLs; the browser service
# also downloads its package manager on first boot. lan: not needed; scraping LAN hosts is an
# opt-in power-user case we do not grant by default.
permissions:
  internet: true
  lan: false

#    working at boot (ioredis/BullMQ speak RESP, which Valkey is wire-compatible with).
#  - rabbitmq and nuq-postgres KEPT as non-root sidecars over pre-chowned relative binds. malmo
#    provisions no managed AMQP type, and nuq-postgres is a custom postgres:17 + pg_cron + nuq.sql
#    image the managed Postgres (15/16, no pg_cron, no init scripts) cannot replace -- so per the
#    gate's bundled-engine row the sidecar IS the intended path. Both official images self-chown
#    their data dir and gosu/privilege-drop ONLY when started as root; the non-root identity from
#    service_user: true makes them skip both and boot clean under cap_drop: ALL. See manifest.yml.
#  - rabbitmq: upstream uses amqp://rabbitmq:5672 with the built-in guest user, which RabbitMQ
#    refuses over a non-loopback connection. We set a named user (firecrawl) + a generated
#    password so the api's cross-network AMQP connection is accepted; NUQ_RABBITMQ_URL carries it.
#  - api ports: "${PORT}:${INTERNAL_PORT}" host mapping DROPPED; the brain owns ingress and routes
#    to the internal listen port (main_port: 3002). extra_hosts (host-gateway), ulimits, and the
#    per-service logging/cpus/mem_limit blocks are local-dev-only and dropped (the brain owns
#    restart, logging, and resource policy).
#  - api command stays the image default (node dist/src/harness.js --start-docker). --start-docker
#    is a NO-OP under compose: harness.ts gates all container-spawning on POSTGRES_HOST != "localhost"
#    (it is nuq-postgres here), logging "Running in docker-compose, skipping ... container management".
#    No docker socket is needed or granted.
#  - USE_DB_AUTHENTICATION stays false. Firecrawl's only auth path is Supabase-backed (needs a
#    Supabase stack malmo does not provide); with it false the API is unauthenticated. On hosted,
#    malmo's per-app owner-only exposure gate (forward_auth in the box Caddy) sits in front by
#    default, so the API is not open to the internet unless the owner deliberately makes the app
#    public. Called out in the manifest description and notes.md.
#  - OPENAI_API_KEY, SEARXNG_ENDPOINT/SEARXNG_ENGINES/SEARXNG_CATEGORIES, and PROXY_* are
#    operator-supplied config: (see manifest.yml). Unset, the LLM (/extract) and /search features
#    are simply off; core scrape/crawl/map are unaffected.

x-common-env: &common-env
  REDIS_URL: ${MALMO_SERVICE_CACHE_DSN}
  REDIS_RATE_LIMIT_URL: ${MALMO_SERVICE_CACHE_DSN}
  PLAYWRIGHT_MICROSERVICE_URL: http://playwright-service:3000/scrape
  POSTGRES_USER: postgres
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${MALMO_SECRET_POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
  POSTGRES_DB: postgres
  POSTGRES_HOST: nuq-postgres
  POSTGRES_PORT: "5432"
  USE_DB_AUTHENTICATION: "false"
  # OPENAI_API_KEY (LLM /extract) and SEARXNG_ENDPOINT (/search) are declared as manifest
  # config: and injected by the brain directly onto this (main) service when the operator
  # supplies them. Unset, Firecrawl reads them as undefined and those endpoints are simply
  # off; core scrape/crawl/map are unaffected. They are intentionally NOT placeholder'd here.

services:
  # --- infrastructure sidecars -------------------------------------------------
  nuq-postgres:
    image: ghcr.io/firecrawl/nuq-postgres:latest
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${MALMO_SECRET_POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB: postgres
    volumes:
      - ./data/nuq-postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres -d postgres"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 60s

  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3.13-management
    environment:
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER: firecrawl
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS: ${MALMO_SECRET_RABBITMQ_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - ./data/rabbitmq:/var/lib/rabbitmq
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "rabbitmq-diagnostics", "-q", "check_running"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 60s

  # --- browser microservice ----------------------------------------------------
  playwright-service:
    image: ghcr.io/firecrawl/playwright-service:latest
    environment:
      # The image's CMD is `pnpm start`, which re-triggers corepack's ensurePackageManager;
      # under service_user's arbitrary non-root uid HOME defaults to `/` and corepack dies on
      # `EACCES: mkdir '/.cache/node/corepack'`, crash-looping the browser service (so scrapes
      # silently fall back to the non-browser fetch engine). Point HOME at the writable tmpfs.
      HOME: /tmp
      PORT: "3000"
      MAX_CONCURRENT_PAGES: "10"
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:size=1g

  # --- the api (the app's single port) -----------------------------------------
  api:
    image: ghcr.io/firecrawl/firecrawl:2.11.120
    environment:
      <<: *common-env
      HOST: "0.0.0.0"
      PORT: "3002"
      ENV: local
      NUQ_RABBITMQ_URL: amqp://firecrawl:${MALMO_SECRET_RABBITMQ_PASSWORD}@rabbitmq:5672
    depends_on:
      nuq-postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      rabbitmq:
        condition: service_healthy
      playwright-service:
        condition: service_started

apps.name: Flipt
apps.short_description: Self-hosted feature flags you toggle at runtime, without redeploying.
apps.long_description:
## Overview
Flipt is an open-source feature-flag and experimentation server that runs
entirely on your own hardware. Wrap a risky change in a flag, then turn it on
or off at runtime from the dashboard instead of shipping a new release. Rules
can target specific users or segments, split traffic by percentage for a
rollout or an A/B test, and every evaluation is served by your own box rather
than a vendor cloud.

## Features
- Runtime feature flags you can toggle without redeploying
- Segment and user targeting, percentage rollouts, and A/B variants
- Namespaces to keep separate projects or environments apart
- REST and gRPC evaluation APIs, plus OpenFeature support, so your own
  services can ask which features are on
- Managed PostgreSQL provisioned automatically, nothing to wire up

## Setting up
Flipt has no built-in username and password login. It signs you in through an
identity provider you already use, so you need to register an OAuth
application with that provider and paste its credentials into this app's
configuration form, either at install or later from the app's page in malmo.

Pick one of the two methods and fill in only that one:

- **GitHub**: create an OAuth app at github.com/settings/developers, then turn
  on "Sign in with GitHub" and enter:
  - Client ID: from your GitHub OAuth app
  - Client secret: from your GitHub OAuth app
- **Single sign-on (OpenID Connect)**: works with Google, Okta, Auth0,
  Authentik, and similar. Turn on "Sign in with a single sign-on provider" and
  enter:
  - Issuer URL: your provider's OpenID Connect issuer address
  - Client ID: from the application you registered with that provider
  - Client secret: from that same application

When your provider asks for a callback or redirect URL, give it this app's
address followed by `/auth/v1/method/github/callback` for GitHub, or
`/auth/v1/method/oidc/sso/callback` for single sign-on.

To let your own services read flags, sign in and create an API token from
Flipt's settings, then give that token to the SDK in your code. Flag reads
are authenticated, so a service without a token cannot evaluate flags.

## Good to know
Until you finish the step above, Flipt installs and runs but nobody can sign
in to the dashboard. That is deliberate: Flipt's own default is to leave its
admin API unauthenticated, which would mean anyone who reached the address
could create or flip flags, so malmo requires sign-in instead. You can add the
credentials at any time from the app's page and the app restarts into a
working state.

Turning a sign-in method on while leaving its fields blank will stop the app
from starting, because Flipt refuses to boot with an enabled but
unconfigured provider. Fill both the toggle and its fields together.

On the appliance this app's address is your home network's `.local` name, which
is plain HTTP. Most single sign-on providers (Google, Auth0, Okta) reject
redirect addresses that are not HTTPS, so single sign-on generally will not
work there and GitHub, which does accept them, is the practical choice. On
hosted, where the address is a real HTTPS URL, both methods work.

This is Flipt's version 1 line. Upstream now steers new users to version 2,
which is published under a licence malmo cannot offer on the hosted tier, so
version 1 is what ships here.
